reading.title: The Night Market
reading.text:
Every Thursday, Omar helped his grandmother at the night market. Her stall sold spices in tall glass jars: golden turmeric, red paprika and tiny black seeds that smelled of lemons.
This Thursday, the market was busier than ever. A man in a smart grey suit stopped at the stall and frowned at the jars. “I need a spice for my restaurant,” he said, “but I don’t know its name. It is the colour of sunset and it makes rice taste like flowers.”
Omar’s grandmother smiled and tapped a small wooden box. Inside were thin red threads. “Saffron,” she whispered. “It is the most precious spice in the market.”
The man sniffed the threads and his frown disappeared. He bought three boxes and shook Omar’s hand. “Your grandmother is a spice detective,” he said.
On the way home, Omar decided that one day he would be a spice detective too.

qs.q: On which day did Omar help at the market?

“the most precious spice” What does precious mean?

c: He had found the spice he wanted.

qs.q: Why did the man call Grandmother a “spice detective”?
qs.a: She worked out which spice he meant.
c: She worked out which spice he meant.

qs.q: Which of these happened first?
c: Omar decided to be a spice detective.

reading.title: How Bees Make Honey
reading.text:
Honeybees live together in large groups called colonies. A colony can have up to 60,000 bees, but only one queen.
Worker bees fly from flower to flower to collect a sweet liquid called nectar. They suck it up with a long tongue and store it in a special stomach. Back at the hive, they pass the nectar to other bees, who chew it and add special juices from their bodies.
Next, the bees spread the nectar into the wax cells of the honeycomb. They fan it with their wings so that the water dries out and the nectar becomes thick. Finally, they seal each cell with a lid of wax.
A single worker bee makes only about one twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life!

c: They seal each cell with wax.

qs.a: to dry it out so it becomes thick
c: to dry it out so it becomes thick

qs.a: to show it is a surprising fact

reading.title: The Robot Who Wanted to Paint
reading.text:
In a busy car factory, there was a robot called Bolt. All day long, Bolt tightened bolts on car doors: twist, click, twist, click. He was fast, he was careful and he never made a mistake.
But Bolt had a secret. At night, when the factory lights went off, he dipped a spare cloth into the leftover paint and painted pictures on the factory wall. He painted the moon over the sea, a field of sunflowers and a camel resting under a palm tree.
One morning, the factory manager, Mrs Haddad, arrived early and saw the wall. Bolt’s motors whirred nervously. Would he be in trouble?
Mrs Haddad stood still for a long time. Then she laughed. “Our factory has been grey for twenty years,” she said. “Bolt, how would you like to paint the whole building?”
Bolt’s lights flashed green, which was the robot way of grinning.

c: He wanted to sell the pictures.

reading.title: Sea Turtles
reading.text:
Sea turtles have lived in the oceans for more than 100 million years. That means they swam in the sea when dinosaurs walked the Earth.
A sea turtle cannot pull its head into its shell like a land tortoise can. Instead, it has strong flippers that help it swim long distances. Some green turtles swim thousands of kilometres between the beaches where they lay eggs and the places where they feed.
A female turtle comes onto a sandy beach at night and digs a nest with her back flippers. She lays around 100 eggs, covers them with sand and returns to the sea. About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and race towards the water.
Today, plastic in the sea is one of the biggest dangers for turtles, because they can mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and eat them.

“the baby turtles hatch” What does hatch mean?

Why does the writer mention dinosaurs?
qs.a: to show how long turtles have been around
c: to show how long turtles have been around
